analysis.one_liner: Taxes half of big bonuses paid by bailed-out banks and puts the money into small business loans.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in December 2009 with no cosponsors, sent to two House committees, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a 50% excise tax on any year-end bonus above $50,000 that a bank or firm that received bailout money (TARP funds) paid to a current or former employee during 2010. The company, not the employee, would pay the tax. The money would go into a new Treasury trust fund, the Small Business Growth Fund, that would pay for a program letting the Small Business Administration make loans directly to small businesses.
analysis.who_benefits: Small businesses that would be able to borrow directly through the SBA, funded by the tax on large bonuses at bailed-out financial firms. Taxpayers who had funded the 2008-2009 bailouts would also see some of the cost of large executive bonuses clawed back.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 50% excise tax, paid by the employer, on the portion of any 2010 bonus above $50,000 paid by a TARP recipient to a current or former employee, including officers and executives.
Routes all revenue from that tax into a Small Business Growth Fund and directs the SBA to run a direct lending program for small businesses modeled on its existing 7(a) loan program.

analysis.who_pays: Financial firms that received federal bailout money and their highest-paid employees, who would lose roughly half of any bonus over $50,000 to the new tax.
analysis.who_pays_short: Bailed-out banks and their bonus recipients

drawbacks.text: The tax applied only during 2010 and only to firms that received TARP money, so it was a one-year measure rather than a lasting rule on Wall Street pay.

An employer-paid tax on bonuses can prompt firms to restructure pay as salary, deferred payouts, or other compensation outside the tax's definition of a bonus, reducing the revenue the bill counts on. This is the standard design problem with excise taxes aimed at a narrow slice of pay.
It is a targeted tax on a specific group of companies; critics of such measures argue it singles out one industry for punishment, while supporters point out those firms were compensated by taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade is straightforward: money from large bonuses at firms taxpayers rescued would fund loans to small businesses. The main honest caveats are that it was a one-year tax, so the small business lending program would have temporary funding, and firms could restructure pay to blunt the tax. It was a modest, narrowly aimed measure, not a broad overhaul of Wall Street compensation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 19, 2009 and referred to the Ways and Means and Small Business committees, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Welch introduced the Wall Street Bonus Tax Act on December 19, 2009, near the end of the first session of the 111th Congress.
The bill attracted no cosponsors at any point.
It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the House Small Business Committee, and to the Small Business Subcommittee on Finance and Tax.
No further action of any kind was taken on the bill for the remainder of the Congress, which ended January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Bailed-out financial firms and their highest-paid employees kept 2010 bonuses free of the proposed 50% tax, and no Small Business Administration direct lending program funded by that tax was created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Bailed-out banks kept their bonuses untaxed

for.name: Rep. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Wall Street Bonus Tax Act on December 19, 2009 and referred it to two House committees.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral (chair: Rep. Charlie Rangel, D-NY)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in December 2009 and never held a hearing or markup on it; the bill died in committee.

against.name: Financial industry
against.role: Banks and financial firms that received TARP bailout funds and their lobbying operations
against.what_they_did: Opposed congressional efforts in 2009-2010 to tax or claw back bonuses at bailed-out firms, the policy environment in which this bill gained no cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no one else signed on, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and committee inaction, not a measurable partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would have cut roughly half of any 2010 bonus over $50,000 at firms that took federal bailout money, with the firm itself paying the tax. Their interest in avoiding it ran against taxpayers who had funded their rescue.
The tax revenue would fund a new SBA direct lending program for small businesses, giving them a public lending channel. The bill never advanced, so this benefit never materialized.

industries.industry: Private bank lenders in SBA programs
industries.note: Direct SBA lending would have competed with private banks that currently originate government-backed small business loans. The competition never happened because the bill died.
